attributes.previous_value: Three published execution benchmarks are linked, alongside the DRAGEN 4.2 developer total runtime for HG002 (1,838.5 seconds). All measure conventional variant-calling pipelines; none measures a genomic foundation model. None prints repeated runs, measured peak memory or accuracy next to runtime, so they do not show reproducibility, and hardware differs within each comparison, so differences mix software and hardware. On ten WGS samples run by a University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital group with no declared competing interests (Samarakoon et al. 2025), read mapping plus HaplotypeCaller for NA12878 (47.55x) took 2,317.7 minutes on a CPU-only GATK pipeline, 123.45 minutes with Parabricks on four L4 GPUs, 78.12 on four A100 GPUs, 54.22 on eight H100 GPUs and 60.29 with DRAGEN v4.2. On the same H100 machine, Parabricks DeepVariant took 14.58 minutes for NA12878 with the version the pipeline used (printed 4.1.0-1; Methods say 4.3.0-1) and 16.05 minutes with the updated version (printed 4.3.0-1; Discussion says 4.3.1-1). On one HG002 30x genome on Google Cloud (O'Connell et al. 2023; the authors' employer funded the study and is an NVIDIA, AWS and Google alliance partner), HaplotypeCaller took 38.8 hours and cost 67.9 USD on a 32-vCPU machine and 0.59 hours and 17.5 USD on eight A100 GPUs, while the somatic caller LoFreq cost 8.1 USD on the CPU machine and 19 to 30.1 USD on 2 to 8 A100 GPUs. On Google Cloud machines of similar hourly cost (Franzoso et al. 2025, no declared conflicts), Sentieon DNASeq took 0:14:00 to 0:16:00 per exome at 0.82 to 1.03 USD and 3:00:00 to 3:50:00 per genome at 8.02 to 10.7 USD, and Parabricks Germline on one T4 GPU took 0:10:00 to 0:14:00 per exome at 0.71 to 0.93 USD and 4:06:00 to 4:40:00 per genome at 8.13 to 10.6 USD; costs exclude the Sentieon licence, and two genome runtime cells that cannot be genome runtimes are disputed and left out of these ranges. Each comparison is one run per sample on at most ten public samples, and costs are list prices at the time of each study.

Only the foundation-model benchmark prints spread over repeated runs (five trials); none reruns a variant-calling pipeline to measure concordance of the calls, none prints variant-calling accuracy in the same table as runtime, and hardware differs within most comparisons, so differences mix software and hardware. On ten WGS samples run by a University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital group with no declared competing interests (Samarakoon et al. 2025), read mapping plus HaplotypeCaller for NA12878 (47.55x) took 2,317.7 minutes on a CPU-only GATK pipeline, 123.45 minutes with Parabricks on four L4 GPUs, 78.12 on four A100 GPUs, 54.22 on eight H100 GPUs and 60.29 with DRAGEN v4.2. On the same H100 machine, Parabricks DeepVariant took 14.58 minutes for NA12878 with the version the pipeline used (printed 4.1.0-1; Methods say 4.3.0-1) and 16.05 minutes with the updated version (printed 4.3.0-1; Discussion says 4.3.1-1). On one HG002 30x genome on Google Cloud (O'Connell et al. 2023; the authors' employer funded the study and is an NVIDIA, AWS and Google alliance partner), HaplotypeCaller took 38.8 hours and cost 67.9 USD on a 32-vCPU machine and 0.59 hours and 17.5 USD on eight A100 GPUs, while the somatic caller LoFreq cost 8.1 USD on the CPU machine and 19 to 30.1 USD on 2 to 8 A100 GPUs. On Google Cloud machines of similar hourly cost (Franzoso et al. 2025, no declared conflicts), Sentieon DNASeq took 0:14:00 to 0:16:00 per exome at 0.82 to 1.03 USD and 3:00:00 to 3:50:00 per genome at 8.02 to 10.7 USD, and Parabricks Germline on one T4 GPU took 0:10:00 to 0:14:00 per exome at 0.71 to 0.93 USD and 4:06:00 to 4:40:00 per genome at 8.13 to 10.6 USD; costs exclude the Sentieon licence, and two genome runtime cells that cannot be genome runtimes are disputed and left out of these ranges. On human WGS at five read depths on the HPC nodes of a regional genome project (Marangoni et al. 2026; the GeNePi developers, no declared competing interests; one unnamed sample per depth), a 30x genome took 17h with the CPU GATK equivalent and 1h 36m, 42 m and 30m with Parabricks v4.3.0 on two V100, two A100 and four A100 GPUs, and a 100x genome 60h, 6h 30m, 2h 30m and 2h 06m. On one 120-vCPU Azure instance (Hu et al. 2026; all authors employed by Sentieon), DNAscope took 18.9 minutes for 30x Illumina, DNAscope LongRead 41.2 minutes for 30x PacBio HiFi and DNAscope Hybrid 85.8 minutes for 10x PacBio HiFi plus 35x Illumina, at 1.1, 2.5 and 5.2 USD on demand excluding the licence; each pipeline had different input data, so the three are not a ranking. For GenomeOcean on one H100 (Yu et al. 2026; two authors are at the DOE Joint Genome Institute, which develops GenomeOcean; GTDB bacterial genomes; mean and standard deviation over five trials), embedding extraction with the 4B model ran at 21,386 ± 126 input tokens per second with 72.14 GB peak GPU memory in BF16 and 22,401 ± 204 with 67.91 GB with FP8 weights, and generation ran at 1818.79 ± 7.95 generated tokens per second in BF16 and 2169.04 ± 24.30 with FP8 weights, activations and KV cache. No active linked result measures variant-calling accuracy against a truth set; the GenomeOcean ARI values score metagenomic binning against GTDB species labels. The two withheld studies are Zheng et al. 2026 (Clair3 developers; Clair3 and DeepVariant on HG003 long reads), whose supplementary runtimes, DeepVariant version and DeepVariant accuracy differ from its Results text and whose accuracy uses one GIAB sample's v4.2.1 confident regions, which leave out the hardest regions; and Aspidova et al. 2026 (ModernGENA and GENA-LM developers; four DNA language model families on one A100), whose printed tokens per second are far too low for its batch sizes. Apart from the five GenomeOcean trials, each comparison prints one value per sample and set-up on at most ten samples, and costs are list prices at the time of each study.

name: Evidence summary: RNA pathogen detection workflows
description: Plain-language summary of what the reviewed evidence shows. Draft until reviewed.

attributes.value: The single-assay results are a UCSF respiratory RNA metagenomic assay at 93.6% (103 of 110) sensitivity against original clinical respiratory panel testing, as reported by its developers, and the developers' own prospective validation of an Oxford nanopore workflow on 344 nasopharyngeal swabs (preprint). With thresholds fixed on a separate derivation set, the nanopore workflow detected 51% (133 of 260) of PCR-positive targets in the samples passing quality control, from 85% for RSV to 19% for rhinovirus/enterovirus, and 99.8% of PCR-negative targets were not detected; criteria chosen after the validation raised sensitivity to 58%, and the authors attributed all nine false positives to barcode crossover. Its swabs were selected mostly as PCR-positive at Ct 30 or below, with about one negative per eight positives, and reads were matched only to the 23 panel pathogens, so it does not test detection outside the panel. Three comparisons of several workflows add proxy evidence. On 88 nasal washings scored against 1144 respiratory virus PCR results (Carbo et al. 2022), all five classifiers detected 22 or 23 of the 24 PCR-positive results at species level at a read-count cut-off chosen on the same data, but 31% to 58% of their positive calls were PCR-negative. When 13 European clinical virology laboratories each ran their own pipeline on the same 13 clinical datasets (de Vries et al. 2021, preprint), 10 to 13 samples were correctly called positive, and the three pipelines that found every sample reported 6, 2 and 0 additional PCR-negative viruses. In the CAMI II blood metagenome challenge (Meyer et al. 2022), 4 of 10 submissions listed the causal virus. In a developer benchmark of five virus profilers on one shared database (Tisza et al. 2026, preprint), the model-estimated probability of reporting the correct family for reads from seven divergent viruses at 10 read pairs was 0.974 for EsViritu and 0.9998 for Metabuli but 0.045 for Kraken2, 0.012 for Centrifuger and 0.0009 for Sylph at the authors' headline settings, and Metabuli reported a median of 18 false species in seven pathogen-free libraries against 0 for EsViritu. None of this is clinical validation: the cohorts are small or single-site, reference databases and reporting rules differ, and the benchmark data are mostly synthetic.
